result:
Race condition: result depends on the timing of concurrent processes touching shared state. With a log: two scripts write at once → interleaved or lost lines.

Single-line appends: use `>>` with one `printf` per line. `>>` opens with `O_APPEND` → kernel seeks to end and writes atomically per `write()`, so short lines from separate processes don't clobber each other on a local filesystem. This breaks when one record spans several writes (multi-line output, a piped command's buffered output), on NFS, or when anything rewrites the file (`>`, `sed -i`, read-then-write) instead of appending.

For those cases, serialize with `flock`:

```bash
{
  flock 9
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -Is)" "$msg"
  some_command            # multi-line output stays contiguous
} >>"$LOG" 9>>"$LOG.lock"
```

Lock releases when the block exits, even on crash, so there is no stale lockfile to clean up. Every writer must take the same lock; one script that skips it reintroduces the race. Avoid check-then-act locking like `[ -f lock ] || touch lock`, which is itself a race.
